column1: # Original WritingDeck exercises; MIT to the extent rights subsist; AI-assisted original drafting. Completion is self-reported, not machine quality judgment.
# stable_id|category|difficulty|minutes|work_mode|requires|excludes|title|instructions

wd-x-0001|dialogue|1|15|drafting|dialogue-only|narration-only,no-spoken-dialogue|An answer with two jobs|Write a conversation in spoken lines only. Give one speaker a practical question and the other a reason to answer a different emotional question. Let the mismatch change what they decide, without explanatory narration.

wd-x-0002|dialogue|2|20|drafting|dialogue-only|narration-only,no-spoken-dialogue|The useful misunderstanding|Write only spoken dialogue between people who understand the same word differently. Both meanings must remain reasonable. End with a practical choice that exposes the difference rather than a speech explaining the misunderstanding.

wd-x-0003|dialogue|2|20|drafting|dialogue-only|narration-only,no-spoken-dialogue|A boundary negotiated|Use spoken lines only to negotiate a small boundary. Neither speaker may simply win. Make each revise an assumption about what the other is asking, and let the final agreement leave one useful detail unresolved.

wd-x-0004|dialogue|3|25|drafting|dialogue-only|narration-only,no-spoken-dialogue|Three incompatible clocks|Write spoken dialogue among three people who need the conversation to finish at different times. Avoid direct statements of their deadlines until the final exchange. Let interruptions and delayed answers reveal the pressure.

wd-x-0005|dialogue|1|10|drafting|dialogue-only|narration-only,no-spoken-dialogue|The repeated question|Write a conversation in spoken lines only in which the same ordinary question appears three times. Change its meaning through the preceding answers, not by changing its wording or adding a narrator's interpretation.

wd-x-0006|dialogue|3|30|drafting|dialogue-only|narration-only,no-spoken-dialogue|A correction nobody wants|Write only spoken lines. One person must correct a minor factual mistake whose correction threatens a comfortable arrangement. Keep the factual point simple, and make the difficulty lie in what acknowledging it would require.

wd-x-0007|description|1|10|drafting|narration-only,visual-detail|dialogue-only,nonvisual-only|A room with a use|Describe a room without quoted speech. Select visible details according to the task someone must perform there. Let an obstacle emerge from the arrangement of objects rather than adding a sentence announcing that the room is inconvenient.

wd-x-0008|description|2|20|drafting|narration-only|dialogue-only|The second inspection|Describe the same object before and after a character learns something important about it. Use no dialogue. Keep the physical object unchanged; alter selection, comparison, and sequence so the second description supports a different decision.

wd-x-0009|description|2|20|drafting|narration-only,visual-detail|dialogue-only,nonvisual-only|An honest inventory|Describe an apparently ordinary collection through visible wear and placement. Do not state its owner's personality. Give each selected detail a practical history that a reader can infer without turning every object into a symbol.

wd-x-0010|description|3|25|drafting|narration-only|dialogue-only|Two scales of damage|Describe a damaged place at two scales: a broad view and one small repairable feature. Use no spoken lines. Make the small feature change what the observer believes can be done next, rather than merely making the description more vivid.

wd-x-0011|description|1|15|drafting|narration-only|dialogue-only|The absent regular|Describe a familiar public place on a day when one regular visitor is absent. Use no dialogue and do not name the absence directly. Show which ordinary activities no longer happen or must be performed by someone else.

wd-x-0012|description|3|30|drafting|narration-only,nonvisual-only|dialogue-only,visual-detail|A place without sight|Describe a place without visual information or spoken dialogue. Let sound, contact, smell, temperature, and bodily effort establish an actionable route. The observer should discover a practical limit, not simply list sensations.

wd-x-0013|point-of-view|1|15|drafting|first-person|third-person|A limited witness|Write in first person about an event the narrator can observe but cannot fully interpret. Give the narrator one confident explanation and include a concrete detail that makes another explanation possible without announcing that the narrator is unreliable.

wd-x-0014|point-of-view|2|20|drafting|third-person|first-person|Knowledge with a boundary|Write close third person from one character's viewpoint. Include another person's decisive action without reporting that person's thoughts. Make the viewpoint character choose what to do using evidence that supports more than one motive.

wd-x-0015|point-of-view|2|20|drafting|| |The peripheral participant|Tell a turning point from the viewpoint of someone doing an ordinary supporting task. Give that task consequences for the central event. Do not let the observer know everything merely because the principal characters are busy.

wd-x-0016|point-of-view|3|25|drafting|multi-scene,time-jumps|single-scene,continuous-time|Two witnesses later|Write two short scenes in which different witnesses remember the same incident on different later days. Each should preserve an accurate detail the other misses. Let the remembered accounts influence separate present decisions rather than compete for a single correct verdict.

wd-x-0017|point-of-view|1|15|drafting|first-person|third-person|What I did not ask|Write a first-person account of a conversation after it ends. Focus on the question the narrator chose not to ask. Give the omission an immediate practical consequence, and distinguish what the narrator knows from what they assume.

wd-x-0018|point-of-view|3|30|drafting|third-person|first-person|Distance at the hinge|Use third person and begin at an observational distance. Move closer to one person's perceptions at a moment of choice, without entering anyone else's thoughts. Make the shift reveal a pressure that the broad view could not register.

wd-x-0019|voice|1|15|drafting|| |A practiced explanation|Write a narrator explaining something they have explained too often. Let rhythm and selection show both expertise and impatience. Add one new detail that forces the explanation to change rather than simply become more irritated.

wd-x-0020|voice|2|20|drafting|| |Certainty with a seam|Write in a voice that sounds confident about ordinary procedure. Introduce a small exception the speaker cannot account for. Keep the voice recognizable while allowing a hesitation, correction, or detour to expose the limit of that confidence.

wd-x-0021|voice|2|20|drafting|| |Affection without praise|Let a narrator describe someone they care for without using direct compliments. Choose practical observations and remembered habits. Include one annoyance that makes the affection more particular rather than canceling or sentimentally excusing it.

wd-x-0022|voice|3|25|drafting|| |A borrowed register|Write someone using a formal register they have learned for a specific occasion. Let it work in one exchange and fail in another. The failure should reveal a difference in purpose, not invite mockery of how the person speaks.

wd-x-0023|voice|1|10|drafting|| |The useful digression|Give a narrator one digression that initially seems unnecessary. Make its concrete information matter to a later choice within the piece. Avoid ending with an explicit statement that the apparent distraction was important all along.

wd-x-0024|voice|3|30|drafting|| |Two honest tones|Write two versions of the same short account, one restrained and one exuberant. Preserve the facts and consequences. Compare what each tone makes easier to admit and what each tends to hide; choose which tension to carry forward.

wd-x-0025|structure|1|15|drafting|single-scene,continuous-time|multi-scene,time-jumps|One uninterrupted task|Write one continuous scene organized around a task that can be completed in the available place. Do not jump in time. Make an interruption change the meaning of finishing, while keeping the physical task visible enough to follow.

wd-x-0026|structure|2|20|drafting|multi-scene,time-jumps|single-scene,continuous-time|Consequence before cause|Begin with a practical consequence, then move to an earlier scene showing the choice that produced it. Give the earlier scene its own uncertainty. Do not let advance knowledge of the outcome remove the characters' reasons to hesitate.

wd-x-0027|structure|2|20|drafting|multi-scene,time-jumps|single-scene,continuous-time|The changed return|Write three brief scenes built around returning to the same place. Change one actionable detail on each return. Let those changes alter a relationship or plan, rather than using the place only as a repeated backdrop.

wd-x-0028|structure|3|30|drafting|multi-scene,nonlinear-order|single-scene,linear-order|A causal braid|Write two strands from different times and alternate between them. Each switch must answer one concrete question while raising another. Give the strands different immediate goals, and let their connection become useful before the final paragraph.

wd-x-0029|structure|1|15|drafting|single-scene,continuous-time|multi-scene,time-jumps|A scene with an exit|Write a single continuous scene in which someone intends to leave. Keep the exit physically possible. Change the reason for staying through what happens, rather than blocking the door or giving a narrator the final explanation.

wd-x-0030|structure|3|30|drafting|multi-scene,time-jumps|single-scene,continuous-time|The omitted interval|Write two scenes separated by an unshown interval. Make the second scene contain evidence of a choice made during the gap. The reader should infer its consequence while remaining uncertain about one important part of its motive.

wd-x-0031|motivation|1|15|drafting|| |A reason that costs|Give a character a simple practical goal and a reason to pursue it. Make the first available method threaten something they also value. Let the choice reveal priorities through action rather than a list of admirable qualities.

wd-x-0032|motivation|2|20|drafting|| |The changed request|Begin with a character asking for something specific. During the exchange, let evidence show that obtaining it would not meet the underlying need. Have the character revise the request without claiming complete self-understanding.

wd-x-0033|motivation|2|20|drafting|| |A generous limit|Write an offer of help made in good faith. Give the helper a limit they have not stated, and let the recipient reasonably rely on the offer. Bring the limit into the open through a decision both must participate in.

wd-x-0034|motivation|3|25|drafting|| |The inherited ambition|Give a character an ambition first chosen to please someone else. Present an opportunity to fulfill it after that person's influence has changed. Let the character separate what remains genuinely wanted from what has become habit.

wd-x-0035|motivation|1|10|drafting|| |A small refusal|Write a minor refusal that matters more to the person making it than to observers. Establish the practical request clearly. Let the refusal protect a value or boundary without requiring a grand speech or a villainous requester.

wd-x-0036|motivation|3|30|drafting|| |Good reasons in collision|Give two people incompatible immediate goals and a defensible reason for each. Let each learn one fact that weakens their preferred solution. End with an action that costs both something different, not with a declaration that both were right.

wd-x-0037|senses|1|10|drafting|nonvisual-only|visual-detail|The route by contact|Describe moving through a short route without visual information. Use contact, balance, sound, and effort to locate obstacles. Make one sensation prompt a specific correction rather than adding sensory details that do not affect movement.

wd-x-0038|senses|2|20|drafting|| |A changed sound|Choose a recurring sound in a place. Establish what someone normally does when hearing it, then alter the sound slightly. Make the change lead to a test or action rather than immediately revealing a hidden danger.

wd-x-0039|senses|2|20|drafting|| |Temperature as information|Use temperature to reveal a practical fact a character has overlooked. Connect the sensation to a cause they can investigate. Avoid treating cold or warmth as an automatic synonym for fear, comfort, or moral character.

wd-x-0040|senses|3|25|drafting|nonvisual-only|visual-detail|A disputed sensory clue|Write two people interpreting the same nonvisual clue differently. Give each relevant experience that supports the interpretation. Let a physical test resolve one aspect while leaving the emotional consequence for them to negotiate.

wd-x-0041|senses|1|15|drafting|| |The familiar smell elsewhere|Place a familiar smell in an unexpected setting. Give the observer a concrete memory and an immediate task. Let the association complicate that task rather than using the memory as an unrelated pause in the action.

wd-x-0042|senses|3|30|drafting|| |Sensation under effort|Write someone performing a physically demanding but ordinary task. Let fatigue change which sensations they notice and trust. Make one mistaken interpretation consequential, without claiming exhaustion makes the person foolish or unreliable in every respect.

wd-x-0043|pacing|1|15|drafting|single-scene,continuous-time|multi-scene,time-jumps|Delay with a purpose|Write a continuous scene in which someone needs a quick answer. Give each delay new information or a changing practical condition. Avoid stretching the moment with repeated gestures that leave the available choices unchanged.

wd-x-0044|pacing|2|20|drafting|| |Fast action, slow recognition|Write an action that happens quickly and a recognition that takes longer. Keep the physical sequence clear. Spend more narrative attention on the consequence that alters a plan than on decorating every movement equally.

wd-x-0045|pacing|2|20|drafting|multi-scene,time-jumps|single-scene,continuous-time|Compress the routine|Move through a repeated routine in a concise passage, then expand one occurrence into a scene. Choose the expansion because a decision becomes possible there, not simply because the day contains a dramatic external event.

wd-x-0046|pacing|3|25|drafting|| |Pressure without a countdown|Create urgency without stating a time limit. Use changing resources, opportunities, or social expectations to narrow the options. Keep the pressure legible through concrete changes, and let a character notice it before a narrator summarizes it.

wd-x-0047|pacing|1|10|drafting|| |A pause that changes things|Insert a pause into a practical exchange. During it, let someone notice information that changes the next action. The pause may be quiet, but it should do more than signal that the characters are having strong feelings.

wd-x-0048|pacing|3|30|drafting|| |Unequal speeds|Write two people carrying out the same task at different speeds. Give each a reasonable method. Let the mismatch create a choice about cooperation, and change sentence rhythm where the practical pace actually changes.

wd-x-0049|setting|1|15|drafting|| |A rule built into a place|Invent or choose a place whose layout enforces an ordinary rule. Show someone trying to accomplish a task there. Let the built environment help one participant and hinder another without explaining the place as a moral lesson.

wd-x-0050|setting|2|20|drafting|| |A service after hours|Set a scene in a public place after its normal service has ended. Give someone a legitimate need to remain. Let the altered lighting, access, or staffing change what can be negotiated, rather than merely making the setting eerie.

wd-x-0051|setting|2|20|drafting|| |Weather with a mechanism|Make weather affect a scene through a specific physical or social mechanism. Show which resource, route, or responsibility changes. Keep the setting consequential without using weather to predict a character's moral worth or future fate.

wd-x-0052|setting|3|25|drafting|| |Two uses of one place|Give the same place two simultaneous legitimate uses that conflict. Ground each use in practical details. Let someone propose an adaptation and discover what that proposal would preserve or remove for each group.

wd-x-0053|setting|1|10|drafting|| |The unadvertised entrance|Describe someone finding an entrance not shown in the official directions. Give it a practical history through use and wear. Let choosing it change who the character meets or what obligation they appear to accept.

wd-x-0054|setting|3|30|drafting|| |A place changed by policy|Choose one ordinary policy change and show its material effects in a place. Follow a character trying to do something simple. Include a benefit as well as a barrier, and make the decision arise from their coexistence.

wd-x-0055|conflict|1|15|drafting|| |One object, two uses|Give two people legitimate plans for the same object. Make neither plan merely symbolic. Let an attempted compromise expose a property of the object or a timing condition that changes what sharing would actually require.

wd-x-0056|conflict|2|20|drafting|| |A fair rule applied|Show someone applying a rule they sincerely believe is fair. Introduce a case where the rule produces a barrier its maker did not anticipate. Let the conflict concern a concrete remedy rather than winning an abstract debate.

wd-x-0057|conflict|2|20|drafting|| |An accurate accusation|Give one character an accurate complaint that omits important context. Let the other supply the context without denying the act. Make the next action depend on what both can acknowledge, not on discovering that the complaint was false.

wd-x-0058|conflict|3|25|drafting|| |A solution that moves the cost|Let a character solve an immediate problem by shifting work or risk elsewhere. Give the affected person a chance to respond. Revise the available solution through that response rather than using the hidden cost as a final twist only.

wd-x-0059|conflict|1|10|drafting|| |The reasonable interruption|Interrupt someone's important task with another person's reasonable need. Establish both stakes quickly. Make the response alter the task or relationship, without relying on one participant secretly being malicious or incompetent.

wd-x-0060|conflict|3|30|drafting|| |A precedent at stake|Write a small decision whose participants disagree about the precedent it creates. Keep the immediate practical problem visible. Let each person identify a different future case, and end with terms precise enough to test later.

wd-x-0061|subtext|1|15|drafting|| |An offer with a question inside|Write someone offering a practical favor while hoping to learn whether they are welcome. Let the recipient respond to both levels imperfectly. Do not state the hidden question directly until the offer has changed what each can do next.

wd-x-0062|subtext|2|20|drafting|| |The object not discussed|Give two people a practical reason to handle an object associated with an unresolved event. Keep their immediate task clear. Let choices about touching, moving, or returning it carry information that their polite words avoid.

wd-x-0063|subtext|2|20|drafting|| |Public agreement, private limit|Write an apparently agreeable exchange in front of an audience. Give one participant a boundary they cannot comfortably announce there. Make the boundary legible through a specific correction or condition rather than coded gestures alone.

wd-x-0064|subtext|3|25|drafting|| |A compliment with consequences|Write a sincere compliment that assigns its recipient a role they no longer want. Let the recipient answer without rejecting the affection. Make the response open a practical possibility rather than merely reveal discomfort to the reader.

wd-x-0065|subtext|1|10|drafting|| |A change of subject|Let someone change the subject for a defensible reason. Make the new topic connected to the avoided one through a practical detail. Give the other person a choice about following the detour or returning to the original question.

wd-x-0066|subtext|3|30|drafting|| |Two versions of reassurance|Write an exchange where each person offers the reassurance they themselves would want. Let a small failure reveal the mismatch. End with one more specific request for care, without requiring either person to explain their entire history.

wd-x-0067|revision|1|15|revision|| |Follow the causal verbs|Work on a separate copy of an existing passage. Mark the actions that change a later choice, then revise one transition whose causal connection is unclear. Preserve the original and note what became easier to infer; completion is your judgment.

wd-x-0068|revision|2|20|revision|| |Remove the repeated explanation|On a separate copy, locate an event explained both through action and through commentary. Try removing one explanation, then read the result for lost context. Keep only the version that supports the intended inference, not automatically the shorter one.

wd-x-0069|revision|2|20|revision|| |Give the other person evidence|Choose a conflict in an existing passage and make a separate copy. Add one observable fact supporting the less-developed participant's position. Revise the response to that fact without making both sides equally correct by decree.

wd-x-0070|revision|3|30|revision|| |Repair a knowledge leak|On a separate copy, identify information the viewpoint character could not yet know. Replace one unsupported certainty with perception, inference, or a later discovery. Check that the replacement changes the next decision coherently rather than only softening a verb.

wd-x-0071|revision|1|10|revision|| |Test the scene's exit|Make a separate copy of a scene ending. Try ending at the last action that changes an available choice, then compare with the original ending. Keep the version that carries the intended uncertainty; do not count fewer words as proof of improvement.

wd-x-0072|revision|3|30|revision|| |Revise the cost, not the adjective|On a separate copy, replace one vague statement of difficulty with a concrete cost, limit, or obstacle. Follow the consequence through the next action. Preserve any useful ambiguity about motive rather than explaining every feeling at once.

wd-x-0073|formal|1|15|drafting|| |A practical lipogram|Choose one letter to avoid and write a short account of an ordinary task without it. Keep an actual choice or obstacle understandable. Review the constraint yourself, and note where it led to a useful new expression rather than claiming the restriction improves all prose.

wd-x-0074|formal|2|20|drafting|| |A growing sentence sequence|Write successive sentences that each add one word compared with the previous sentence. Choose and record your starting length. Let the growth accompany a changing practical situation; count using your chosen word rule and treat the result as an experiment.

wd-x-0075|formal|2|20|drafting|| |A small working vocabulary|Choose a limited vocabulary before drafting and keep the list beside you. Use it to tell a complete practical encounter. Afterward, mark where the restriction sharpened action and where it hid necessary distinctions; no automatic vocabulary checker is implied.

wd-x-0076|formal|3|30|drafting|| |Three forms, one decision|Write the same small decision as a list, a letter, and a scene. Preserve the practical facts in all three versions. Compare what each form lets a speaker omit, then choose one omission worth exploring further.

wd-x-0077|formal|1|10|drafting|| |The repeated concrete word|Choose one concrete word and repeat it at three structurally important points. Change its practical reference or consequence each time. Avoid explaining the repetition's symbolism; test whether its placement helps the reader follow a changed relationship.

wd-x-0078|formal|3|30|drafting|multi-scene,nonlinear-order|single-scene,linear-order|A reversible sequence|Write three brief scenes that can be read forward and backward. Preserve understandable actions in both orders, but let the inferred motive differ. Label the two reading orders and compare them yourself; the app does not claim to validate the formal effect.

wd-x-0079|read-through|1|10|read-through|| |Read for unanswered practical questions|Read an existing passage without changing it. List the practical questions it asks a reader to hold, and mark where each is answered or intentionally left open. Choose one question for later review; this is self-reported analysis, not measured editing.

wd-x-0080|read-through|2|20|read-through|| |Trace who knows what|Read an existing scene and make a separate note of what each participant knows at its start and end. Identify one inference that depends on evidence in the scene. Record a possible revision without silently changing the original.

wd-x-0081|read-through|2|20|read-through|| |Listen for identical turns|Read a conversation aloud or silently attend to its rhythm. Mark adjacent turns doing the same practical job. Decide whether the repetition creates pressure or merely restates information, and record one possible experiment in a separate note.

wd-x-0082|read-through|3|25|read-through|| |Audit the hidden labor|Read a scene for work that enables its central action: preparation, travel, care, maintenance, or cleanup. Note who performs it and who benefits. Choose one omission whose clarification could change a decision, without treating a tally as a quality score.

wd-x-0083|read-through|1|15|read-through|| |Check the physical route|Read a scene while sketching its movements in a separate note. Identify where access, distance, or an object's placement affects a choice. Mark any uncertainty for review; the sketch is a reading aid, not authoritative story fact.

wd-x-0084|read-through|3|30|read-through|| |Read against the favored account|Choose a passage with a strong viewpoint and read for evidence that complicates its preferred explanation. Record one defensible alternative using only what is present. Do not call the alternative a proven fact or automatically replace the existing account.
